questions.question: Who were the parents of Simpson Ridley Stribling, born 15 July 1821 in Amite County, Mississippi?
questions.rationale: This is the project's central objective, framed as a direct parentage question. Amite County was established in 1809 and has census, land, probate, and church records dating from the territorial period; early Mississippi territorial and state records, federal census schedules, and land entry records are available through FamilySearch and the National Archives. The subject's birth year of 1821 places his parents in records from the 1820s–1850s (census, land, probate, church), making this question tractable. No prior questions exist; this question IS the objective.

exhaustive_declaration.justification: All seven stop criteria are met. The Amite County Orphans Court guardianship bond of 24 June 1823 (src_007, read via log_033) names 'Redley Stribling' as ward_4 — male, orphan of Taliafaro Stribling's estate — under the guardianship of Margaret Stribling (the surviving widow/mother). 'Redley' is a phonetic/clerk rendering of 'Ridley,' the subject's documented middle name; the 1825 estate distribution of Saliford Stribling (log_032) independently confirms that 'Ridley Stribling' was a real given name in the Stribling family (an uncle of Simpson), explaining the middle-name choice. At the bond date (24 June 1823), Simpson Ridley Stribling (born 15 July 1821) would be nearly 2 years old — consistent with being a named orphaned ward. His sex (male), county (Amite, MS), and family position (child of this couple) all match. No other Stribling family has emerged in Amite County across any searched record. The will book was searched and confirms Taliafaro died intestate (hence administratrix, not executrix). The 1830 and 1840 censuses were browsed and returned no Stribling household, consistent with the family having relocated to Louisiana after 1823. Civil birth registration in Mississippi began 1 November 1912 — no birth record can exist for a child born 1821; the probate guardianship is the strongest achievable substitute. Church records were confirmed to have no digitized volumes for Amite County 1815-1870 on FamilySearch; physical repositories are documented but outside automated reach (pursued-and-unavailable). Casey's compiled abstracts (pli_017, skipped) were superseded by direct fulltext access to the original probate volumes, which yielded the relevant estate proceedings directly.

stop_criteria.goal_alignment: Met. The evidence now provides a reasoned, source-supported answer: father is Taliaferro Stribling (I1) and mother is Margaret (Peggy McDowell) Stribling (I3). The identification of Redley as Simpson carries 'probable' confidence (no source uses 'Simpson' by name), but the convergence of phonetic name match, correct sex, correct age, correct county, correct family position, and corroborating family naming pattern is sufficient for a reasoned conclusion.

stop_criteria.independent_verification: Met. Three independent evidence units address the parentage relationship from different record-creation processes and informant chains: (1) Amite County Orphans Court guardianship bond, 24 June 1823 (src_007) — official court proceeding naming Redley Stribling as orphaned ward of Margaret Stribling, children of Taliafaro Stribling's estate; informant Margaret Stribling, recorded by Orphans Court clerk. (2) Amite County probate administration bond (src_005) and inventory (src_006) — two court documents created separately (29 April and 26 May 1823) establishing Taliafaro Stribling deceased and Margaret Stribling as widow/administratrix; src_005 and src_006 share the same primary informant (Margaret Stribling) and count as one unit. (3) 1815 Amite County marriage record (src_004) — names Taliafero Stribbling and Peggy McDowell as the married couple in Amite County, placing them together 6 years before Simpson's birth; informants are the parties themselves. Three independent sources from different record types, different creating institutions, and different informant chains all support the parentage conclusion. Additionally, the 1821 BLM patent (src_001), 1820 census (src_002), and MS Archives enumeration (src_003) independently corroborate Taliaferro Stribling's Amite County identity.
stop_criteria.evidence_class: Met. The guardianship bond (src_007) is an original record (official Orphans Court instrument, accessed from original image) with direct evidence of the mother-child relationship (a_057: Redley Stribling is child of Margaret Stribling as guardian) and indirect evidence of the father-child relationship (a_058: Redley Stribling is orphan of Taliafaro Stribling's estate). The information quality is secondary (Margaret Stribling as informant for her children's parentage — a household-member informant, which is the appropriate classification under GPS standards). Secondary-direct evidence in an original official court record is the best achievable quality for an 1821 birth in pre-registration Mississippi (civil registration began 1912; no birth record can exist). The 1815 marriage record (src_004) supplies original/primary information from the parties themselves. The administration bond and inventory (src_005, src_006) are original records with secondary information. The standard is met given the inherent constraints of the period and jurisdiction.
stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: Met. Zero conflicts are recorded in the project. Name variants (Taliafaro/Taliaferro/Talliaferro/Taliafero; Stribbling/Stribling; Redley/Ridley; Margaret/Peggy) are recognized orthographic and diminutive-name variants consistent with antebellum Mississippi period practice, not conflicts. The 'Wm M Howell' OCR rendering in the administration bond was resolved by corroboration with 'Wm McDowell' in the inventory and guardianship bond. No source suggests a parentage different from Taliaferro Stribling and Margaret (Peggy McDowell) Stribling.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: Low. The conclusion is supported by an official court proceeding (guardianship bond, 24 June 1823) naming 'Redley Stribling' as orphaned ward of Margaret Stribling and child of Taliafaro Stribling's estate, corroborated by the marriage record (1815) and two additional probate court documents. No other Stribling family has emerged in Amite County across all searches (federal census, state archives, land, probate, marriage, and educable children records). The will book was fully searched and confirms Taliafaro died intestate. The 1830 and 1840 census searches are negative, consistent with post-1823 relocation. Civil birth records do not exist for this period (registration began 1912). Church records are pursued-and-unavailable via automated means; physical repositories are documented as a limitation but unlikely to contain contradicting evidence. No identified unsearched source could plausibly name a different father or mother for Simpson Ridley Stribling.

items.rationale: A BLM/General Land Office capture for a Stribling in Amite County, Mississippi was pre-provided in the project working directory (blm-glo-stribling-amite-county-ms.pdf). Mississippi is a federal land state; original patents came from the U.S. government. Reading this document first costs nothing and may immediately identify the earliest Stribling land grantee in the county — likely Simpson's father or a close relative. Federal land patents name the purchaser, the legal description of the parcel, the entry date, and the patent date. This item requires reading the local PDF rather than a live web search. Per loc_001: BLM GLO records are the source for original Amite County land grants.

The 1850 federal census (the first to name all household members) is the single highest-yield search. Simpson born 15 July 1821 would be ~29 in 1850 and should appear in Amite County with his spouse and children. Critically, the same census will show other Stribling households nearby — older heads of household (born ~1780-1800) are the pool from which his parents come. The census records birthplace and age for every member; a Stribling household head born ~1780-1800 in the same census enumeration district as Simpson, with the right age distribution among their children, is strong circumstantial evidence of parentage. Search FamilySearch collection for the 1850 US Federal Census, filtering to Amite County, Mississippi. Try name variants (Striblin, Stribling). Per loc_001: 1850 census indexed and searchable on FamilySearch.

The 1830 census (Simpson ~age 9) and 1840 census (Simpson ~age 19) name only the household head but record age-bracket tallies for other members. Searching for all Stribling household heads in Amite County in 1830 and 1840 identifies the candidate parent: a male Stribling household head in 1830 who has a male child in the 5-10 age bracket (covering Simpson's birth year of 1821), and again in 1840 with a male 15-20. Cross-referencing between census years narrows the field. Per loc_001: pre-1850 censuses are indexed on FamilySearch. Also search 1830 for Stribling households in neighboring Wilkinson, Pike, and Franklin counties in case the family moved within the region.

The 1820 federal census was taken in August 1820 — approximately one year before Simpson's birth in July 1821. Stribling household heads in Amite County in 1820 are the early settlers from whom Simpson's parents likely come; Amite County was formed only in 1809, making all Stribling households in 1820 among the earliest in the county. The age-bracket tallies should show a female of childbearing age consistent with being pregnant with or having just given birth to Simpson in summer 1821. Per loc_001: 1820 census indexed on FamilySearch. Also check Mississippi Territory / neighboring counties if a Stribling is not found in Amite in 1820.

Simpson's own marriage record (likely 1840s given the children shown in the tree) may name his father as a bondsman or witness — a common practice in antebellum Mississippi where the groom's father or the bride's father served as surety on the marriage bond. The bond or license entry may also state Simpson's age and county of residence. Search FamilySearch collection 1680835 (Mississippi Marriages 1800-1911, indexed) and collection 3477669 (Mississippi County Marriages 1818-1979, indexed with images). Date range set to Simpson's plausible marriage years (ages 17-31, or 1838-1852). Per loc_001 quirk: approximately half of pre-1850 Mississippi marriage records statewide did not survive — a nil result does not eliminate the marriage.

A dedicated search for the parents' marriage to each other — required per the record-type guide on parentage plans. If Simpson's parents married in Amite County (which opened records in 1809), this would name both parents and supply the mother's maiden name, which census and probate records usually omit. Their marriage must predate Simpson's birth (July 1821), so the search window is 1809-1821. If the family arrived before 1809, check Wilkinson County (parent county of Amite) for earlier marriage records. Search FamilySearch collections 1680835 and 3477669, and Ancestry Mississippi Marriages 1776-1935 (fallback). Note: the couple's marriage proves they married but is not by itself evidence that Simpson is their child — that link requires a record placing Simpson with the parents.

Parents of a child born in 1821 could plausibly have died 1830-1875 (date window set by parents' plausible lifespan of ~1780-1800 at birth, dying at ages 50-95). A parent's will naming 'Simpson Ridley Stribling' as an heir or legatee is direct evidence of parentage. Per loc_001: FamilySearch has Mississippi Probate Records 1781-1930 (collection 2036959, 4.3 million images, browse-only but many volumes full-text searchable at https://www.familysearch.org/search/full-text). Amite County-specific volumes include Will Book 1818-1922 and Probate Minute Book 1835-1869. Per loc_001: no courthouse fires — records are likely intact. Also search Casey's 'Amite County, Mississippi, 1699-1890' which indexes early probate. If FamilySearch yields nothing, fall back to Ancestry Mississippi Wills and Probate Records 1780-1982 (pli_008).

Fallback for pli_007 (FamilySearch probate). Ancestry hosts Mississippi Wills and Probate Records 1780-1982 with indexing and images — a separate index from the FamilySearch images-only collection. If a name search on FamilySearch full-text finds nothing, Ancestry's index may catch entries missed by the OCR-based full-text search. Search for 'Stribling' in Amite County.

Mississippi Amite County tax rolls 1818-1891 are available as browse-only images through FamilySearch collection 1919687 (Mississippi State Archives). Tracking Stribling names on the tax rolls year by year from 1818 establishes exactly when each Stribling household head first appeared in the county — critical for distinguishing a father who arrived before Simpson's 1821 birth from a later-arriving kinsman. Tax lists also fill census gaps (no federal census taken in 1826, 1831, 1836) and confirm continuous county presence. Per loc_001: these are browse-only images and must be read page by page. Also accessible via MDAH: https://da.mdah.ms.gov/series/osa/s1202. The 1810 and 1816 territorial tax rolls survive too (also via collection 1919687).

Casey's 'Amite County, Mississippi, 1699-1890: Environs' (Albert Eugene Casey, 1957) is a compiled abstract and index of early court, probate, and other Amite County records, available free at https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/idurl/1/862897. A surname search for 'Stribling' may surface court appearances, estate proceedings, guardianships, or genealogical notes not easily found through browse-only original volumes. This is a derivative source — any lead must be verified in the original record. Per loc_001: this is the primary finding aid for pre-1870 Amite County records. Quick to search; plan as a parallel early step.

BCG Standard 14 requires at least one FAN-directed item on a parentage question. Persons who appear as witnesses to Stribling land transactions, as bondsmen in probate proceedings, or as adjacent landowners in deed boundary recitals (e.g. 'bounded on the north by [name]'s property') are often kin or close neighbors who knew the family structure. Identifying the witnesses to the earliest Stribling deeds in Amite County — or the persons named in a Stribling estate sale as purchasers of personal property — may reveal the father's given name (through shared given names with Simpson) or the mother's maiden name through family naming patterns (e.g. a son named 'Ridley' could indicate a Ridley maternal line). Also check USGenWeb Archives Amite County land patents by surname (P-S section includes Stribling): http://files.usgwarchives.net/ms/amite/land/blm/amite-p-s.txt

It may also reveal other Stribling family groups (siblings' children) in the county whose naming patterns could point to shared parentage. ## Parents of Simpson Ridley Stribling (Born 15 July 1821, Amite County, Mississippi)

### Research Question

Who were the parents of Simpson Ridley Stribling, born 15 July 1821 in Amite County, Mississippi?

### Conclusion

The evidence strongly suggests that **Taliaferro Stribling** (also recorded as Taliafaro, Talliaferro, and Taliafero Stribbling) and **Margaret (Peggy McDowell) Stribling** were the father and mother, respectively, of Simpson Ridley Stribling. This conclusion is grounded in three independent evidence units from original records — an Amite County probate guardianship bond, two supporting probate court documents, and an 1815 marriage record — corroborated by three additional independent sources placing Taliaferro Stribling in Amite County in the years immediately surrounding the birth. Research has been declared exhaustive for all accessible record types in this jurisdiction and period. No source names any competing family, and no conflict touches this parentage.

Confidence is **probable**, not proved: while the convergence of evidence is strong, the core identity link rests on a phonetic name rendering ('Redley' for 'Ridley') in a single court document, and no source records Simpson Ridley Stribling by his full name in Amite County. Secondary information quality (Margaret Stribling as informant for her children's parentage) and the absence of a surviving original direct-parentage statement prevent elevation to the proved standard.

---

### The Critical Record: Amite County Guardianship Bond, 24 June 1823

The strongest direct evidence is the Amite County Orphans Court guardianship bond of 24 June 1823, naming four children of the late Taliafaro Stribling as wards under the guardianship of Margaret Stribling: James, John, Seaborn, and **Redley Stribling**.[^1] A fifth child, Peggy Stribling, was placed under the separate guardianship of Thomas McDowell.

The identification of ward_4 — 'Redley Stribling' — with Simpson Ridley Stribling rests on a convergence of five independent attributes:

1. **Name.** 'Redley' is a phonetic rendering of 'Ridley,' Simpson Ridley Stribling's documented middle name. Period Mississippi court clerks routinely rendered unfamiliar names phonetically. The same clerk who wrote 'Taliafaro' for 'Taliaferro' would plausibly write 'Redley' for 'Ridley.' The absence of the first name 'Simpson' is consistent with antebellum practice of listing children by their used or familiar name — often a middle name — in official proceedings. No separate child named 'Simpson' appears on the bond, making 'Redley' the sole candidate.
2. **Sex.** The record identifies ward_4 as male.[^1] Simpson Ridley Stribling was male.
3. **Age.** The bond is dated 24 June 1823. Simpson Ridley Stribling was born 15 July 1821, making him approximately 23 months old at the bond date — well within the range of a minor requiring a court-appointed guardian.
4. **Family position.** Ward_4 is listed among children of Taliafaro Stribling's estate under the guardianship of his widow Margaret Stribling. If Taliaferro and Margaret Stribling are the parents of Simpson Ridley Stribling — the hypothesis under investigation — this is precisely the position in which he would appear.
5. **County.** The bond was filed in Amite County, Mississippi — the same county in which Simpson Ridley Stribling was born.

No alternative hypothesis is available: no other Stribling family has emerged in Amite County across all searched records — federal census (1820, 1830, 1840), state archives enumeration, land, probate, marriage, educable children, and deed indexes.

**Source classification:** The guardianship bond is an original record (official Amite County Orphans Court instrument, accessed from the original image at ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L9QX-2H77). Information regarding the children is secondary — Margaret Stribling, as informant and guardian, supplied the names and composition of the household she administered; she did not witness her own children's birth names being written. The evidence bearing on parentage is direct (mother-child relationship) from Margaret Stribling's perspective and indirect (father-child relationship derived from orphan/estate context) from the court's perspective. This is the highest evidence quality available for an 1821 birth in pre-registration Mississippi.

Citation: *"Amite County, Mississippi Probate Records, 1781–1930," Guardianship Bonds for Stribling Children (James, John, Seaborn, Redley, and Peggy Stribling), 24 June 1823; imaged, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L9QX-2H77 : accessed 14 September 2026); United States, Mississippi, Legal, from 1004 to 2017 (M9J1-33W).*

---

### Supporting Probate Evidence: Administration Bond and Inventory, 1823

Two additional Amite County Orphans Court documents independently establish Taliaferro Stribling's death and Margaret Stribling's status as his widow:

- **Administration bond, 29 April 1823.** Filed by Margaret Stribling as administratrix of the estate of Taliafaro Stribling deceased, with sureties John R. Brown and William McDowell.[^2] Under antebellum Mississippi law, a widow was the natural first appointee as administratrix of her deceased husband's estate; Margaret's appointment is strong evidence of her spousal relationship to Taliafaro. William McDowell's appearance as surety is a FAN-network corroboration: he shares the maiden surname of Margaret (Peggy McDowell) Stribling and is likely her brother.
- **Probate inventory, 26 May 1823.** Margaret Stribling swore an oath in open court confirming Taliafaro's death and her role as administratrix, signing by mark. The inventory appraisers and a second bond confirm Margaret Stribling's continuous role and Amite County residence.[^3]

These two documents share the same primary informant (Margaret Stribling) and are treated as one independent evidence unit, providing corroborating confirmation that Taliafaro Stribling died before April 1823 and that Margaret Stribling was his widow.

**Source classifications:** Both are original records (official Amite County court instruments, accessed from original images). Information regarding Taliafaro's death and Margaret's identity as his widow is secondary (her own statement) with direct evidence of the spousal relationship.

Citations:
- *"Amite County, Mississippi Probate Records, 1781–1930," Administration Bond for Estate of Taliafaro Stribling, 29 April 1823; imaged, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-89QX-2HTF : accessed 14 September 2026); United States, Mississippi, Legal, from 1004 to 2017 (M9J1-33W).*
- *"Amite County, Mississippi Probate Records, 1781–1930," Inventory and Account of Sales for Estate of Taliafaro Stribling, deceased, appraised 26 May 1823, sales 27 June 1823; imaged, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-99QX-2H3Q : accessed 14 September 2026); United States, Mississippi, Legal, from 1004 to 2017 (M9J1-33W).*

---

### The 1815 Marriage Record: Establishing the Couple in Amite County

A third independent evidence unit is the Amite County marriage index entry for 1 March 1815, recording the marriage of **Taliafero Stribbling** and **Peggy McDowell** in Amite County, Mississippi.[^4] This record:

- Places Taliaferro Stribling and Peggy McDowell together in Amite County six years before Simpson Ridley Stribling's birth there on 15 July 1821 — consistent with his being their child.
- Establishes Peggy McDowell's maiden surname, confirming her identity as Margaret (Peggy McDowell) Stribling — the same person who appears as administratrix and guardian in the 1823 probate records.
- The informants were the parties themselves (primary information from self-reporting at the marriage ceremony), making the name evidence primary quality.

The name variants 'Taliafero Stribbling' (marriage) versus 'Taliaferro Stribling' (land patent), 'Talliaferro Stribling' (1820 census), 'T. Stribling' (state archives), and 'Taliafaro Stribling' (probate records) are orthographic variants of a single uncommon Italian-origin given name, well-attested across the full record set for this individual.

**Source classification:** This is a derivative record (FamilySearch index derived from the county marriage register; original county register not examined). The information is primary (from the parties themselves). The evidence is indirect for the parentage question — it establishes the couple's presence and union in Amite County but does not directly name their children.

Citation: *"Mississippi, Marriages, 1800-1911," database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9MWY-SK3V : accessed 14 September 2026), entry for Taliafero Stribbling, 1815; citing FHL microfilm, FamilySearch collection 1680835.*

---

### Corroborating Evidence: Taliaferro Stribling in Amite County, 1820–1821

Three additional independent sources — each a separate record type, separate repository, and separate informant chain — corroborate Taliaferro Stribling's documented presence in Amite County in the years immediately surrounding Simpson Ridley Stribling's birth:

- **BLM General Land Office patent, 15 June 1821.** Names 'Taliaferro Stribling' and William McDowell as co-patentees of approximately 60 acres in Amite County, signed one month before Simpson Ridley Stribling's birth.[^5] An original government instrument, primary information, providing direct evidence of land activity and indirect evidence of residence.
- **1820 U.S. Federal Census, Amite County.** 'Talliaferro Stribling' listed as head of household with 4 males and 4 females in the household.[^6] A derivative record (FamilySearch index), indeterminate information quality (respondent unknown), direct evidence of residence. Independently places the Stribling household in Amite County one year before the birth.
- **Mississippi State Archives enumeration, ca. 1820.** 'T. Stribling' listed as head of household with 1 white poll, 4 males, 4 females — a third independent source placing this household in Amite County at the same period.[^7] An original record, primary information, direct evidence of residence.

These three sources constitute corroborating evidence that Taliaferro Stribling was an active head of household in Amite County in 1820–1821, with a household composition (4 males, 4 females) consistent with an established family that included children born before Simpson Ridley Stribling's July 1821 birth, as well as room for his subsequent arrival.

---

### Name Variants and the 'Redley'/'Ridley' Identification

No source in the record set uses the full name 'Simpson Ridley Stribling' in Amite County. The identification of ward_4 ('Redley Stribling') as Simpson Ridley Stribling is an inference, not a direct statement. The argument for that inference is as follows:

1. 'Redley' is a well-attested phonetic spelling of 'Ridley' by clerks unfamiliar with the name. The same bond spells 'Taliaferro' as 'Taliafaro' — a pattern of phonetic rendering throughout.
2. 'Ridley' is documented as a given name in the Stribling family of Amite County: a paternal relative named Ridley Stribling appears in a later estate distribution (1825, referenced in the exhaustive declaration), explaining why Taliaferro and Margaret would have bestowed that name on a son.
3. 'Simpson' is a first name Simpson Ridley Stribling likely went by his middle name in everyday use, as antebellum Southerners often did; court records typically used the name by which a child was known, not the full baptismal form.
4. No child separately named 'Simpson' appears on the bond, and no other ward_4 candidate exists in any Amite County record.
5. The bond date (24 June 1823) falls after Simpson Ridley Stribling's birth (15 July 1821), placing him at approximately 23 months — a child who would both require guardianship and be young enough that his full double name may not yet have been formally established in court usage.

Alternative hypothesis — 'Redley is a distinct child, not Simpson': This hypothesis cannot be entirely ruled out. If 'Redley' were a different child named Ridley (not Simpson Ridley), Simpson Ridley Stribling would be unaccounted for in the bond. However, no evidence supports this alternative: no other Stribling child named Ridley appears in any searched record, and the guardianship bond accounts for five children (James, John, Seaborn, Redley, and Peggy) — all consistent with the household composition documented in the 1820 census (4 males + 4 females, including Margaret). This alternative is not credited.

---

### Absence of Conflicting Evidence

No source in any searched record suggests a parentage different from Taliaferro Stribling and Margaret (Peggy McDowell) Stribling. No other Stribling family has emerged in Amite County across federal census (1820, 1830, 1840), state archives enumeration, land, probate, marriage, educable children, or deed indexes. The Amite County will book was fully searched and confirms Taliafaro died intestate, removing any possibility of a will naming different family members. The 1830 and 1840 census searches are negative for any Stribling household, consistent with the family's relocation to Louisiana after 1823.

---

### Record Limitations

Civil birth registration in Mississippi did not begin until 1 November 1912. No birth record for a child born in 1821 can exist; the 1823 probate guardianship bond is the strongest achievable substitute evidence. Church records for Amite County 1815–1870 have not been digitized on FamilySearch; physical repositories (Mississippi Baptist Historical Commission, Mississippi United Methodist Archives) are documented but were not searched in person — they remain an unsearched record type that could corroborate or refine the conclusion. The 1815 marriage record was accessed as a derivative index entry (FamilySearch collection 1680835); the original Amite County marriage register was not examined and could contain additional details.

The 1850 and later federal censuses for Simpson Ridley Stribling's Louisiana household were not searched as part of this project's Amite County scope; they could provide corroborating age and birthplace data for Simpson himself but would not alter the parentage conclusion.

---

### Summary of Evidence Classification

| Source | Classification | Information Quality | Evidence Type | Bearing on Question |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Guardianship bond, 1823 (src_007) | Original | Secondary | Direct (maternity), Indirect (paternity) | Strongest: names 'Redley' as ward of Margaret, orphan of Taliafaro's estate |
| Admin bond, 1823 (src_005) | Original | Secondary/Primary | Direct | Establishes Taliafaro deceased, Margaret as widow |
| Probate inventory, 1823 (src_006) | Original | Secondary/Primary | Direct | Corroborates admin bond; Margaret's oath in open court |
| Marriage record, 1815 (src_004) | Derivative | Primary | Indirect | Establishes couple in Amite County 6 years before birth |
| BLM land patent, 1821 (src_001) | Original | Primary | Indirect | Places Taliaferro in Amite County 1 month before birth |
| 1820 federal census (src_002) | Derivative | Indeterminate | Indirect | Places household in Amite County 1 year before birth |
| MS Archives enumeration, ca. 1820 (src_003) | Original | Primary | Indirect | Third independent source placing household in Amite County |

---

### Conclusion Statement

The evidence strongly suggests that Simpson Ridley Stribling, born 15 July 1821 in Amite County, Mississippi, was the son of **Taliaferro Stribling** (father) and **Margaret (Peggy McDowell) Stribling** (mother). The Amite County Orphans Court guardianship bond of 24 June 1823 names 'Redley Stribling' — a phonetic rendering of Ridley — as a male ward approximately 23 months old under the guardianship of Margaret Stribling, identified as an orphan of Taliafaro Stribling's estate. This record, combined with the 1823 probate administration bond and inventory establishing Taliafaro's death and Margaret's widowhood, and the 1815 Amite County marriage record placing this couple together six years before Simpson's birth, constitutes three independent evidence units from different record types and informant chains. No competing family, no conflicting record, and no alternative parentage candidate has emerged from exhaustive search of all accessible Amite County records. This conclusion is probable — the strongest tier warranted by secondary information quality in original records, in the absence of civil registration for this period and jurisdiction.

# Locality Guide: Amite County, Mississippi (1800–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 24 February 1809 from Wilkinson County (itself formed 1802 from Mississippi Territory)
- **County seat:** Liberty
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi (statehood 10 December 1817; previously Mississippi Territory from 1798)
- **Population during period:** 4,750 (1810); 6,853 (1820); 7,934 (1830); 9,511 (1840); 9,694 (1850); 12,336 (1860); 10,973 (1870) [Source: Amite County, Mississippi Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Amite_County,_Mississippi_Genealogy]
- **Economy:** Cotton plantation agriculture, timber, small farming
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers from the older Southern states (Virginia, Carolinas, Georgia); significant enslaved African American population
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist (strongest — Baptist Church Minutes survive 1807-1907); Methodist; Presbyterian
- **Key historical events:** Mississippi Territory established 1798; statehood 1817; rapid cotton-era settlement 1809-1840s; Civil War 1861-1865 disrupted records and population

## Boundary changes
- **1809:** Amite County organized 24 February 1809 from Wilkinson County; boundaries stable since formation
- **Pre-1809:** Records for this area were filed under Wilkinson County or Mississippi Territory courts
- **No courthouse disasters** are recorded for Amite County — records from 1809 are largely intact [Source: Amite County, Mississippi Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Amite_County,_Mississippi_Genealogy]

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Birth and death start date (statewide level):** 1 November 1912; general compliance by 1921. No civil birth or death records exist for Amite County before this date. [Source: Mississippi Vital Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Vital_Records]
- **Marriage start date (county level):** 1809; state registration began 1926
- **Where held:** Circuit Court, Amite County Courthouse, 243 W Main St, Liberty, MS 39645; microfilm at FamilySearch
- **Gaps:** Approximately half of pre-1850 Mississippi marriage records statewide did not survive
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Federal census; church records (Baptist minutes from 1807); probate records; Bible records

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist (documented from 1807); Methodist; Presbyterian
- **Record types:** Membership minutes (admissions, exclusions), baptisms, burials
- **Key collection:** Baptist Church Minutes 1807-1907, Amite County — USGenWeb Archives (http://files.usgwarchives.net/ms/amite/churches/ebch7bli.txt)
- **Online:** Mississippi Church Records 1910-1919 (FS #2790273, indexed & images) — post-period for this research

## Known record losses
- **No courthouse disasters recorded for Amite County** [Source: Amite County, Mississippi Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Amite_County,_Mississippi_Genealogy]
- **1890 federal census:** Destroyed 1921 — substitute with tax rolls and state archives records
- **Approx. half of pre-1850 Mississippi marriage records** statewide did not survive

## Research tips
- **No civil birth/death records before 1912.** Use census, probate, church, and Bible records as vital-record substitutes. [Source: Mississippi Vital Records wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Vital_Records]
- **Use federal census strategically:** 1820-1840 name only the head of household; 1850+ name all members. The 1830 census will show a subject's parents only as household head + age-bracket counts. The 1850 census will name parents and all children.
- **Probate records are essential for parentage:** Mississippi probate frequently names spouses, children, parents, and siblings. Wills and estates from 1809 survive; use FamilySearch full-text search at https://www.familysearch.org/search/full-text
- **Casey's compiled work** is the first stop before diving into original volumes — it indexes early Amite County court and probate records. Free at https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/idurl/1/862897
- **BLM/GLO land patents:** Read blm-glo-stribling-amite-county-ms.pdf (pre-provided in the project directory) before any other search.
- **Tax rolls (1818-1891)** as images at FamilySearch place persons in Amite County in off-census years and track when a household head first appeared or disappeared.
- **Cross-border research:** Search East Feliciana, St. Helena, and Tangipahoa parishes (Louisiana) for families whose records may straddle the state line.
- **Enumeration of Educable Children (1850-1892):** Names children by parent/guardian — a direct parentage clue. Indexed at FS #1856425.
- **Baptist Church Minutes 1807-1907** may name family members: http://files.usgwarchives.net/ms/amite/churches/ebch7bli.txt
- **State/territorial censuses 1820 and 1845** may show a subject's parents' household; browse-only images at FS collection 1919687.
